data.title: Beacon Financial Earnings Call Balances Progress and Pressure
data.description:
Beacon Financial Corporation ((BBT)) has held its Q3 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call.

Beacon Financial Corporation’s latest earnings call struck a cautiously optimistic tone, blending solid core performance with clear acknowledgment of ongoing headwinds. Management highlighted stable profitability, expanding net interest margin, improved efficiency, stronger capital, and tangible progress in reshaping the loan book. Yet they were frank that GAAP earnings, returns, and overall performance still trail the ambitions laid out in the merger plan.

Profitable Quarter Underscored by Diversified Model

Beacon reported third-quarter GAAP net income of $61.2 million, or $0.73 per share, and operating earnings of $64.7 million, or $0.77 per share. Executives emphasized that the results reflect a diversified business model and consistent profitability, even as the environment remains competitive and capital-intensive.

Promotion

  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks
Learn more about TipRanks Premium

Net Interest Margin Continues to Expand

Net interest income rose $3.9 million sequentially to $197.2 million, with net interest margin widening 4 basis points to 3.85%. Loan yields climbed 14 basis points to 6.13%, while funding costs increased just 1 basis point, and management now sees NIM holding in a 3.85% to 3.9% range.

Operating Revenue and PPNR Momentum

Operating pre-provision net revenue increased 4% from the prior quarter, signaling underlying earnings strength. Noninterest income remained steady across wealth management, loan-level derivatives, and service charges, giving Beacon multiple revenue streams beyond spread income.

Efficiency Gains from Merger Integration

Beacon’s core efficiency ratio improved to 53.5%, which management tied directly to operational momentum following merger integration. Executives noted that the bank has delivered the expense targets set in its merger-of-equals plan, reinforcing the benefits of scale and cost discipline.

Capital Strength Bolstered by Debt Actions

Tangible common equity rose to 9.35% of tangible assets, while the total risk-based capital ratio reached 14.6%. Beacon issued $175 million of 10-year subordinated debt at 6.25% and retired $75 million of higher-cost floating-rate debt, lowering funding costs while reinforcing capital flexibility.

Share Repurchases and Dividend Support Capital Return

The board approved another $75 million in share repurchases, bringing total authorization to $125 million, roughly 5% of market value. A quarterly dividend of $0.3225 per share, equating to about a 4.7% yield, was reaffirmed, with management signaling commitment to both distributions and balance-sheet strength.

Commercial Loan Growth and CRE De-Risking

Commercial and industrial lending grew 1% sequentially and 4% on an annualized basis for the second straight quarter. Beacon also cut its investor commercial real estate concentration ratio to 295%, below its sub-300% merger goal, after more than $500 million of runoff that management now sees largely behind it.

Healthy Loan Pipeline Positions Growth

Management highlighted roughly $610 million of anticipated net new funding in the fourth quarter, excluding paydowns and amortization. Beacon intends to deploy this capacity into high-quality, properly priced credits, suggesting scope for controlled loan growth despite competitive pressure.

Credit Quality Described as Strong and Managed

Executives characterized credit quality as strong, well managed, and stable, with criticized and classified loans declining over the quarter. Roughly half the portfolio was credit marked at merger close, providing a cushion as the bank works through today’s credit environment.

Reserve Coverage Remains Solid

Beacon’s reserve coverage ratio stood at 132 basis points of loans and leases, with about $70 million in specific reserves and $350 million in substandard loans. Management noted that significant charges have already been taken on that substandard bucket, supporting confidence in current loss coverage.

Strategic Push to Grow Fee Income

Fee revenue now accounts for around 11% of total revenue, but Beacon aims to lift that share to the mid teens over time. Opportunities include cash management, Clarendon Private wealth offerings, payments, and SBA loan sales through 44 Business Capital, all targeted as organic growth levers.

Organic Growth and Talent Investments

Growth will focus on relationship-led lending in C&I and owner-occupied commercial real estate, rather than acquisitions. Management plans to add middle-market bankers, build out proven verticals, and pursue selective team lift-outs to deepen client-facing talent and fee-generating capacity.

Deposit Strategy Shifts Toward Core Relationships

Beacon aims to reduce reliance on wholesale borrowings while improving its deposit mix and growing core relationship balances. Market-facing and private banking teams, along with its digital deposit engine, are seen as scalable routes to deepen funding and lessen sensitivity to rate volatility.

Technology and Digital Banking as Growth Enablers

The company plans to leverage merger-driven technology to bring more branch functionality into digital channels and improve always-on client access. Management also sees real potential to use artificial intelligence responsibly to boost operational efficiency and support its workforce.

Branch and Platform Optimization Efforts

Organizational simplification, branch-network optimization, and platform streamlining remain priorities, but not at the expense of growth or client service. In dense markets Beacon will lean into digital servicing, while in less dense areas it will emphasize banker-led private banking and remote channels.

Retention of Employees and Clients in Focus

Top-quartile employee and client retention is a stated goal, with management expressing confidence in current talent and regional leadership, including Boston and Rhode Island. Executives indicated that retention metrics are tracking well, anchoring stability during strategic transition.

Sequential GAAP Earnings Decline from Nonrecurring Items

GAAP net income dipped to $61.2 million from $64.4 million, with EPS falling to $0.73 from $0.77 quarter over quarter. The decline mainly reflected one-time CEO transition costs and the absence of a prior-period gain from selling three facilities.

Reported Returns Ease but Core Metrics More Stable

Return on average assets slipped 6 basis points to 1.11%, and return on tangible common equity fell sharply to 12.02%. Excluding nonrecurring items, core operating ROA was a more resilient 1.17%, with ROTCE at 12.69%, closer to management’s medium-term ambitions.

Balance Sheet Contracts Amid Deposit and Loan Declines

Total assets shrank $375 million to $21.9 billion, as cash and equivalents dropped $445 million and loans fell $170 million to $17.7 billion. Deposits declined $303 million to $18.2 billion, driven largely by a $327 million reduction in payroll deposits, underscoring funding mix shifts.

Loan Paydowns and Competitive Conditions Weigh on Growth

Management said new loan originations have been offset by paydowns and regular amortization, muting net growth. The market remains intensely competitive, with thin spreads and some rivals offering aggressive pricing, though Beacon expects paydowns to slow as rates stay higher.

Nonperforming Loans Tick Up on Two Large Credits

Nonperforming loans rose by about $8 million, reaching 91 basis points of total loans. The increase was driven by two sizable real estate exposures, one an office property in Connecticut facing tenant roll and improvement needs, and the other an industrial asset in Boston being worked out via a possible short sale.

Credit Costs Elevated as Problem Assets Are Resolved

Net charge-offs totaled $13.5 million, or 30 basis points annualized, with provision expense of $8.9 million in the quarter. Management expects credit costs to remain elevated as specific reserves and problem assets are addressed, even while maintaining solid coverage on the broader portfolio.

Operating Costs Rise on Marketing and Fraud

Operating expense, excluding restructuring and intangibles, ticked up to $119.5 million from $118.9 million. Higher marketing, loan-servicing, and fraud costs drove the increase, with fraud up about $600,000 and marketing outlays expected to accelerate in the fourth quarter.

Performance Still Trailing Merger-Plan Targets

Management acknowledged that Beacon has not yet reached the performance levels envisioned in its merger-of-equals blueprint. A mid-teens return on tangible common equity remains the near-term objective, with more precise timelines to come once the strategic plan is finalized.

Operating Environment Remains Challenging

Executives stressed that the backdrop is still difficult, with heightened sensitivity to rate shifts over the last one to two months. Funding costs, loan and deposit mix, pricing discipline, and the ongoing work through problem credits will remain center stage as Beacon navigates the next phase.

Guidance Points to Margin Stability and Organic Growth

Looking ahead, management expects net interest margin to stay in the 3.85% to 3.9% band, aided by roughly $12 million per quarter of purchase accounting accretion. Beacon anticipates about $610 million of net new funding in the fourth quarter, aims to grow fee income into the mid teens percentage of revenue, lower its expense run rate, modestly reduce reserves over time, maintain the dividend, and pursue up to $125 million in buybacks while targeting a mid-teens ROTCE and strong employee and client retention.

Beacon’s earnings call painted a picture of a bank that is profitable, capital-strong, and steadily improving its efficiency, yet still working to fully realize its merger-era promises. Investors will watch closely to see whether Beacon can convert its healthy pipeline, digital investments, and fee-growth plans into higher returns, while managing credit risk and competitive pressure in a challenging rate and funding environment.

data.description:
Columbia Banking System ((COLB)) has held its Q3 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call.

Columbia Banking System’s latest earnings call struck an upbeat tone, with management emphasizing stronger profitability, a net interest margin above 4%, solid deposit growth, and broad fee income gains. Executives balanced this optimism with frank discussion of loan balance declines, competitive lending headwinds, slightly lower capital ratios, and more modest margin guidance for the coming quarter.

Strong Quarterly Earnings and Returns

Columbia reported third-quarter EPS of $0.78 and operating EPS of $0.82, underscoring a solid earnings performance despite a challenging rate and credit backdrop. Return on average assets reached 1.4%, while return on tangible common equity topped 17%, signaling robust profitability and efficient use of shareholder capital.

Promotion

  • Unlock powerful investing tools with TipRanks Premium to make smarter, more confident investment decisions
  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks

Operating Profitability Continued to Improve

Management highlighted sequential and year-over-year gains in operating pre-provision net revenue and net income, driven by a better mix of loans and funding and tight cost control. The addition of PAC Premier to the year-over-year comparison further boosted performance, showing benefits from recent M&A activity.

Net Interest Margin Held Above 4%

Third-quarter net interest margin came in at 4.11%, and after adjusting for one-time items, expanded by 12 basis points sequentially. Management expects NIM to remain above 4% in the fourth quarter, guiding to roughly 4.05%, which still positions Columbia near the top tier of regional bank margins.

Wholesale Funding Cut to Support Margin

Strong customer deposit inflows enabled Columbia to reduce wholesale funding by $1.5 billion between June 30 and September 30. That pullback, including lower public wholesale balances, eased funding costs and contributed meaningfully to the bank’s margin expansion story.

Customer Deposits Showed Strong Growth

Total deposits rose to $52.7 billion from $52.1 billion, with customer deposits increasing by nearly $1.2 billion in the quarter. Seasonal balance growth and new client wins drove the increase, while the average cost of interest-bearing deposits edged down by 1 basis point to 1.95%, reflecting disciplined pricing.

Commercial Relationship Mix Improved

Commercial loans, including owner-occupied commercial real estate, climbed to 43% of the total portfolio from 42% in the prior quarter and 39% a year ago. Loan originations totaled $1.2 billion, and nearly 70% were commercial, underscoring Columbia’s focus on relationship-based business lending.

Fee Businesses Delivered Broad-Based Growth

Fee income engines performed well, with treasury management revenue up 7% year over year and international banking up 19%. Commercial card revenue rose 23%, merchant card grew 11%, and wealth management added to noninterest income, diversifying earnings away from pure spread income.

Noninterest Income Hit the High End of Guidance

Third-quarter noninterest income reached $80 million on a GAAP basis and $87 million on an operating basis, landing at the high end of management’s guided range. Executives expect noninterest revenue to remain in the mid-$80 million range during the fourth quarter, suggesting continued strength in fee-generating businesses.

Expense Discipline and Cost Savings

Operating noninterest expense held steady at $365 million compared with the prior quarter, highlighting tight cost management. The bank identified $132 million to $133 million of PPBI-related cost savings, ahead of its $127 million target, and expects fourth-quarter noninterest expense excluding CDI amortization to fall to $330 million to $335 million.

Credit Metrics Remained Stable

Provision expense totaled $33 million, but management characterized credit metrics as stable and healthy overall. Allowance coverage stood at 1.02% of total loans, or 1.25% including credit discounts on acquired loans, suggesting a conservative posture amid uncertain macro conditions.

Capital Returned Aggressively to Shareholders

Over the past year, Columbia returned more than $1 billion to shareholders via dividends and buybacks, underscoring confidence in its capital generation. In the third quarter alone, it repurchased 6.5 million shares for about $200 million, reducing the common share count by 8% over the life of the program.

New $1.2 Billion Repurchase Authorization

The board approved a fresh $1.2 billion share repurchase program, extending Columbia’s capital return story. Management expects fourth-quarter buybacks to remain in the $150 million to $200 million range and said it intends to fully utilize the authorization, subject to market conditions.

Smooth PAC Premier Integration

Marking the first anniversary of the PAC Premier deal, executives described the integration as the smoothest in the CEO’s two-decade tenure at Columbia. Notably, commercial deposit growth from the former Southern California franchise represented nearly half of total commercial deposit growth in the quarter.

Ongoing Investment in Balance Sheet and Franchise

Columbia continues to invest in technology, automation, infrastructure, and talent while seeking efficiency offsets to protect margins. The bank opened a branch and financial hub in Utah, added a Las Vegas branch, and deepened capabilities in Utah and Arizona, Native American banking, fast-food franchising, treasury management, and wealth management.

Technology and Relationship Banking Expansion

Management highlighted the use of technology, including Salesforce-driven next-best-offer tools, relationship reviews, and working-capital assessments to deepen client ties. About 58% of commercial customers now use treasury management services, indicating growing penetration of higher-fee, stickier products.

Stable Deposit Mix and Beta Outlook

Noninterest-bearing deposits held steady at 33% of total balances, and management expects to maintain that mix going forward. Executives cited a 50% through-the-cycle deposit beta as a reasonable assumption and reported CD rollover rates north of 80%, supporting funding stability.

Long-Term Margin and Commercial Lending Outlook

Columbia expects to operate with a low-4% NIM over the next several quarters, aided by continued optimization from transactional loans toward core relationship-based commercial lending. Commercial and industrial loan growth is seen in the low to mid single-digit range, barring a major macroeconomic setback.

Loan Balances Declined Modestly

Total loans slipped to $46.9 billion from $47.2 billion, reflecting Columbia’s unwillingness to match aggressive competitor pricing and structures. Elevated payoffs in commercial real estate also weighed on balances, though management noted the pace of decline slowed versus the prior quarter.

Average Earning Assets Contracted

Average earning assets were $59.8 billion in the third quarter, signaling modest contraction tied to balance sheet optimization and ongoing CRE payoffs. While the pullback trims asset growth, it supports margin resilience by shedding less attractive exposures.

Fourth-Quarter NIM Guidance Slightly Lower

Management guided to fourth-quarter NIM of around 4.05%, below the reported 4.11% in the third quarter, reflecting conservative expectations. The forecast factors in modest negative carry from excess subordinated debt and typical seasonal deposit outflows later in the quarter.

Competitive Lending Conditions Remain Intense

Executives pointed to irrational competition in some real estate markets, including high leverage, nonrecourse terms unsupported by property cash flows, and rates near SOFR plus 100 basis points. Columbia has chosen to walk away from such deals, prioritizing prudent underwriting over short-term volume.

Provision Expense Driven by Portfolio and Macro Factors

The $33 million provision reflected loan runoff, credit migration trends, and updates to the economic forecast embedded in credit models. Management emphasized that reserve movements were tied mainly to the rate environment and modeled expectations for future hikes, rather than any specific portfolio problem.

CET1 Ratio Declined Slightly

Columbia’s CET1 ratio dipped to 11.5%, as regular dividends and heavy buybacks modestly outpaced strong capital generation and optimization benefits. Even with the decline, the bank remains well capitalized, giving it room to navigate future volatility.

Tangible Book Value and Capital Ratios Under Pressure

Tangible book value slipped to $18.10, driven largely by higher other comprehensive losses as interest rates moved sharply upward. Management also expects total risk-based capital ratios to fall by about 50 basis points after redeeming roughly $240 million of junior subordinated debentures.

Seasonal and Macroeconomic Uncertainty

The bank anticipates seasonal deposit outflows in the second half of the fourth quarter, a normal pattern that will weigh slightly on funding. Future loan and margin trends remain tied to the broader macro backdrop, including potential stress on some real estate and other borrowers from higher interest rates.

Forward-Looking Guidance and Outlook

Looking ahead, Columbia expects NIM around 4.05% in the fourth quarter and staying above 4%, with low-4% margins projected into early next year and potential gradual expansion. Management guided to mid-$80 million noninterest revenue, fourth-quarter noninterest expense of $330 million to $335 million excluding CDI amortization, flat to slightly down loan balances into Q1, low to mid single-digit C&I growth, a steady 33% noninterest-bearing deposit mix, CD rollover rates above 80%, modest 2027 expense growth, and full use of its $1.2 billion repurchase authorization within targeted capital levels.

Columbia Banking System’s earnings call painted a picture of a bank leaning into profitability, fee diversification, and disciplined capital deployment while refusing to chase risky loan growth. With margins still strong, expenses contained, and capital being actively returned, investors will now watch how management balances cautious credit stance with growth ambitions in a shifting rate environment.

data.title: First Citizens BancShares Lifts Outlook After Strong Quarter
data.description:
First Citizens BancShares, Inc. Class A ((FCNCA)) has held its Q3 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call.

First Citizens BancShares struck an upbeat tone on its latest earnings call, as management highlighted earnings that topped expectations, broad-based loan and deposit growth, and healthier credit trends. While they acknowledged competitive pressures, warrant-income volatility, and a temporary funding drag as FDIC debt is refinanced, the overall message was one of confident, disciplined growth.

Earnings Beat Underpins Double-Digit Returns

Adjusted net income reached $652 million, with adjusted earnings per share of $55.37, as returns hit 12.24% on equity and 1.08% on assets. Management emphasized that performance ran ahead of internal expectations, reinforcing the bank’s ability to convert balance-sheet momentum into strong profitability.

Promotion

55% Off TipRanks

  • Unlock powerful investing tools with TipRanks Premium to make smarter, more confident investment decisions
  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks
Learn more about TipRanks Premium

Revenue and Net Interest Income Move Higher

Adjusted net revenue rose 1.4% from the prior quarter, generating positive operating leverage as income grew faster than costs. Net interest income increased by $43 million, helped by higher earning-asset volumes, better yields, reduced borrowings, and a small lift from calendar effects.

Net Interest Margin Holds Firm in a Tough Market

Headline net interest margin came in at 3.07%, while NIM excluding accretion was 2.99%, essentially unchanged from last quarter. Management called this margin stability excellent, especially given industry-wide funding pressures and the ongoing shift in the bank’s liability mix.

Loan Book Expands at an Accelerated Pace

Period-end loans rose by $6.2 billion, or 4.1% sequentially, fueled by high-quality demand across commercial and general banking. The bank also folded in roughly $650 million of loans from the BMO branch acquisition, adding both volume and geographic breadth.

Fund Banking Posts Exceptional Double-Digit Growth

Fund banking loans surged by $4.4 billion, or 11%, as utilization climbed to about 40% and capital-call balances increased with higher transaction activity. The franchise booked nearly $6 billion of new deals in the quarter, underscoring its leverage to private-market capital flows.

Innovation Banking and Verticals Extend Reach

Innovation banking loans rose 6.6% to $10.1 billion, supported by technology-sector demand, referrals from commercial finance, and strategic partnerships. Management highlighted opportunities across working capital, technology, media and telecom, and energy, where specialized verticals are gaining traction.

Deposits Rise Broadly Across the Franchise

Period-end deposits climbed by $11.8 billion, or 6.8%, while average balances increased by $8.0 billion, reflecting broad-based inflows. The bank also absorbed $4.9 billion of deposits from the BMO deal, enhancing its funding base and liquidity profile.

Direct Bank and Innovation Deposits Gain Momentum

The direct bank attracted $3.2 billion of granular, heavily insured retail deposits that management described as high quality and sticky. Innovation banking deposits added another $1.7 billion, helped by a stabilizing startup ecosystem, capital deployment, and new client wins.

BMO Deal Adds Scale, Deposits, and Loans

The BMO branch acquisition brought in about $4.9 billion in high-quality deposits and expanded the branch footprint across 11 states. In addition to liquidity, the transaction contributed roughly $650 million in loans, supporting both balance-sheet growth and market presence.

Client Funds Increase on Innovation and Fund Banking

Total client funds at period-end rose by $6.9 billion, while averages climbed $7.2 billion over the quarter. The increase was driven largely by the innovation and fund banking businesses, reinforcing their growing role in the bank’s funding ecosystem.

Core Fee Lines Stay Resilient Despite Noise

Adjusted non-interest income dipped slightly but still beat guidance, as core fee categories performed well. Lending-related fees grew by $10 million, client investment fees by $9 million, and Rail rental income by $10 million on strong utilization and favorable repricing.

Expense Discipline Bends the Cost Curve

Adjusted non-interest expense was broadly stable and within guidance, despite ongoing digital and data-center investments. Lower professional-services spending, better marketing efficiency in the direct bank, and essentially flat personnel costs helped improve operating efficiency.

Credit Metrics Continue to Improve

Nonaccrual loans fell by $80 million to 0.87% of total loans, and net charge-offs were $103 million, with the loss ratio improving to 0.27%. This ratio has now declined for four straight quarters to its lowest level since early 2023, while criticized and classified assets also moved lower.

Allowance and Credit Outlook Remain Conservative

The bank modestly reduced its loan-loss allowance as credit trends improved but stressed that reserves remain prudent. The allowance covered quarter-to-date net charge-offs more than 3.4 times and year-to-date losses over 3 times, as full-year net charge-off guidance was tightened to 29 to 31 basis points.

FDIC Note Prepayments Cut Debt Load

First Citizens prepaid $8 billion of the FDIC Purchase Money Note during the quarter and another $1.5 billion in October. Since late 2025, the bank has retired about 47% of the original balance, amounting to $17 billion of debt reduction and a structurally stronger balance sheet.

Capital Returns Ramp as CET1 Target Is Met

The company returned $600 million via share repurchases in the third quarter, bringing its CET1 ratio to 10.24%, within the target range. By late October, roughly 24% of outstanding shares had been bought back for $6.9 billion, and a new $1.2 billion repurchase plan is slated to begin in 2027.

Guidance Raised for Loans, Deposits, and Income

Fourth-quarter loan guidance was lifted to $158 billion to $161 billion and deposits to $189 billion to $192 billion, reflecting confidence in continued growth. Full-year guidance for net interest income rose to $6.68 billion to $6.75 billion, while non-interest income expectations increased to $2.22 billion to $2.26 billion.

Margin and Growth Outlook Stays Positive

Management expects headline net interest income to rise by low-single digits in the fourth quarter, with ex-accretion NII growing low to mid-single digits. Looking to the fourth-quarter 2027 exit versus 2026, both headline and ex-accretion NII are projected to increase by mid to high-single-digit percentages.

Expense Growth to Stay in Check

Over the medium term, management sees expenses rising at a low to mid-single-digit pace, helped by ongoing platform and process optimization. For the near term, fourth-quarter expenses are guided to $1.35 billion to $1.39 billion and full-year expenses to $5.39 billion to $5.43 billion.

Fund Banking Economics Remain Compelling

Fund banking loans are delivering spreads slightly above the overall portfolio, while related deposits come in below the bank’s average funding cost. Management noted that spread compression has slowed and that pricing decisions carefully weigh risk-adjusted returns across the full relationship.

Venture and Capital Deployment Stay Active

Sponsors remain flush with dry powder, and fundraising has stayed solid among established managers, supporting ongoing deal activity. Venture investment through the third quarter was described as robust, with little evidence that higher rates are dampening enthusiasm for deployment.

Brand Alignment Lands Smoothly with Clients

The unified brand rollout has generated positive client feedback, with customers focused mainly on consistent service and product offerings. According to management, the market has largely treated the name change as a non-event, with no discernible disruption to relationships.

Regulatory Backdrop Seen as Supportive

Recent and proposed regulatory actions, including Federal Reserve and FDIC initiatives, were described as aligned with the bank’s strategic goals. Management characterized the overall regulatory environment as highly constructive and potentially favorable for future mergers and acquisitions.

Potential Basel III Rules Offer Capital Upside

Under proposed Basel III standardization, the bank estimates a mid to high single-digit reduction in risk-weighted assets, boosting CET1 by around 70 basis points. Including accumulated other comprehensive income is not expected to be material, given the relatively short duration of the investment portfolio.

Non-Interest Income Hit by Warrant Valuations

Adjusted non-interest income fell by $11 million sequentially, largely because warrant income dropped $37 million on valuation marks. Management framed this as a market-driven fluctuation rather than a shift in core franchise performance or client activity.

Higher Funding Costs and FDIC Note Replacement Drag Margin

Rising funding costs offset part of the benefit from higher earning-asset volumes and yields, constraining margin expansion. As the FDIC note is replaced with FHLB borrowings, brokered deposits, or market debt at similar or higher costs, the bank expects a temporary drag on margin.

Fund Banking Growth Expected to Moderate

Management anticipates fund banking utilization easing from the roughly 40% level reached in the third quarter, leading to slower loan growth. They stressed that utilization trends are largely outside the bank’s control and driven by client deployment patterns.

Competition and Spread Pressure Persist in Fund Banking

Competition in fund banking remains intense, and the bank has experienced spread compression over the last six to eight quarters. While the pace of compression has slowed, management does not expect competitive pressures to disappear in the near term.

IPO and Exit Activity Still a Headwind

Despite some improvement, one large transaction accounted for about half of third-quarter exit value, underscoring uneven activity. Management noted that IPO thresholds remain high and that a broadly open IPO window has yet to emerge, limiting capital round-trips for clients.

Client Cash Burn and Onboarding Timing Temper Deposits

Normal client cash burn in the innovation portfolio offset a portion of deposit inflows, adding some noise to growth figures. Institutional onboarding timelines and lower in-transit balances also introduced quarter-to-quarter variability in deposit levels, particularly in the commercial bank.

Rate-Hike Benefits Arrive with a Lag

Because deposits reprice before some variable-rate loans, a portion of the benefit from potential fourth-quarter rate hikes will show up later. Management expects a meaningful share of net interest income upside to materialize in early 2027 rather than in late 2026.

Near-Term Expenses to Tick Higher Seasonally

Fourth-quarter guidance incorporates seasonally higher benefits costs, stronger incentive compensation tied to performance, and elevated professional fees for key projects. The bank also plans a modest uptick in marketing spending to support its growing deposit pipeline.

Guidance Signals Confident Growth with Discipline

Management’s guidance calls for continued loan and deposit expansion, with fourth-quarter loans projected at $158 billion to $161 billion and deposits at $189 billion to $192 billion. Net interest income, fee income, and expenses are all expected to grow within tightly defined ranges, while ongoing FDIC note prepayments and modest debt issuance underpin a measured balance-sheet strategy.

The overall message from First Citizens’ earnings call was one of constructive optimism grounded in conservative risk management. Investors heard a story of stronger earnings, disciplined expense control, improving credit, and rising capital returns, offset by competitive fund-banking dynamics and a near-term funding drag that management believes it can navigate successfully.

Over the past 12 months, loans grew $2 billion, or 14.6%, and deposits rose $2.1 billion, or 13.8%, while the lower-yielding securities portfolio fell by $258 million. Excluding First Savings and a second-quarter mortgage sale, organic loan growth was $473.7 million, or 3.5%, reflecting a deliberate shift toward higher-yielding lending.

Loan Pipeline and Commercial Production

Management expects loan growth to continue in the fourth quarter at a mid-single-digit pace. Commercial production remained healthy across community and corporate banking, asset-based lending, and investment real estate, with pipelines described as stable to modestly higher in several business segments.

Deposit Growth and Relationship Expansion

The loan portfolio’s yield rose 12 basis points sequentially to 6.23%, aided by disciplined pricing in new originations and renewals. Fresh and renewed loans carried an average yield of 6.34%, up from 6.28% in the prior quarter, helping sustain the overall yield despite competitive pressures.

Investment Portfolio Cash Flow for Loan Growth

The bond portfolio declined $168 million in the quarter to $3.1 billion, reflecting paydowns, maturities, and valuation changes. Over the next 12 months, expected cash flows of $271.4 million at a roll-off yield of about 2.11% are set to be redeployed into higher-yielding loans, reinforcing margin and earnings.

Stable Customer-Related Fee Income

Noninterest income totaled $38 million, up $800,000 from the prior quarter, supported by steady customer-related fees of $34.3 million. Growth in service charges, wealth-management fees, and card-payment activity offset a modest decline in gains on loan sales, keeping fee income stable.

New Fee Verticals and Future Growth Outlook

Management highlighted new fee-income streams from SBA lending and first-lien HELOCs that were absent a year earlier. Looking ahead to 2027, client-related fee categories are expected to grow in the high single digits, roughly 8% to 10%, providing a diversified revenue boost beyond interest income.

Strong Capital Position and Capital Return

First Merchants completed a $100 million subordinated debt issuance in late September, lifting total risk-based capital by 60 basis points to 13.58%. Common equity tier 1 capital stood at 11.22% and tangible common equity at 8.83%, and the bank has repurchased nearly 1.3 million shares for $50.3 million year to date, with more buybacks expected.

Diversified Credit Portfolio and Concentration Controls

Total loans reached $15.6 billion, with commercial real estate at 182% of risk-based capital and construction at 42%, comfortably below regulatory concentration thresholds. Shared national credit exposure fell to $936 million across 88 borrowers, while sponsor finance stood around $811 million across 91 companies, illustrating controlled risk.

Credit Losses Largely Previously Reserved

Net charge-offs on two commercial credits matched specific reserves set in the second quarter, meaning losses were largely anticipated. The largest charge-offs and the two sizable relationships moved to nonaccrual this quarter had been previously evaluated and reserved, and provision expense was a manageable $3.3 million.

Long-Term Shareholder Value Creation

Over the past decade, earnings per share have grown at an 8.5% compound annual rate, with dividends rising even faster at 13.3% annually. Tangible book value per share excluding AOCI increased at 8.5% and total assets expanded at 11.2% per year, underscoring a sustained record of shareholder value creation.

Continued Investment in Growth Capabilities

Management said the bank is investing in marketing, branding, technology, talent, and teams built out over the past 18 months to support future growth. It is also actively assessing potential banker hires in Michigan in the wake of regional bank consolidation, aiming to capitalize on market disruption.

Strategic Continuity and Leadership Transition

CEO Mark Hardwick will retire at year-end, with Mike Stewart stepping in as his successor and pledging continuity with the existing leadership team. A fresh strategic planning initiative will focus on sharpening resource allocation and sustaining growth in EPS and tangible book value.

Modest Third-Quarter Loan Growth

Third-quarter loan growth slowed to a 1.8% annualized pace after a strong second quarter, which management described as more modest than desired. Normal payoffs in sponsor finance and shared national credit portfolios largely offset new production, keeping overall commercial balances relatively flat.

Year-to-Date Deposit Decline and Temporary Balances

Total deposits fell at a 0.5% annualized rate year to date, mainly due to balance-sheet repositioning and the removal of First Savings brokered deposits. A sizable commercial deposit inflow from a client’s business sale proved temporary, with funds later shifted to private-client accounts and partially distributed.

Soft Consumer Mortgage Demand

Consumer mortgage activity has softened as borrowing rates near 7%, dampening refinancing and moderating home purchase loans. Even so, management noted that the mortgage pipeline remains at a solid level relative to a year ago, suggesting the business has stabilized rather than stalled.

Interest Rates Reshaping Commercial Decisions

Higher interest rates are prompting some real estate projects to be reconsidered and causing business owners to rethink capital spending and acquisition plans. While certain investment real estate borrowers are feeling pressure, management stressed that rate impacts are not yet translating into widespread credit problems.

Elevated Credit Activity and New Nonaccruals

The bank recorded about $29 million of charge-offs tied to an authorized wireless retailer and a roofing contractor. Two larger relationships, an auto-parts distributor and a digital-marketing firm, moved to nonaccrual, and management acknowledged credit activity remains elevated as it works through a limited set of known issues.

Higher Criticized and Classified Loans

Criticized and classified loan balances rose somewhat during the quarter, though management framed this as normal migration rather than a single large problem exposure. Higher interest rates are affecting parts of the investment real estate portfolio, but without signs of broad deterioration so far.

Tangible Book Value Impact from AOCI

Tangible book value per share fell $0.94, or 3.2%, to $28.86 in the quarter, while the tangible common equity ratio slipped 16 basis points to 8.83%. Both moves were driven by the impact of higher rates on accumulated other comprehensive income, not by underlying operating weakness.

Higher Operating Expenses

Noninterest expense climbed to $116.3 million, exceeding prior guidance as marketing, employee health-insurance costs, and a $500,000 lease impairment pushed spending higher. Excluding $900,000 of acquisition-related charges, expenses rose $3.9 million, and management views the third-quarter run rate as a reasonable base for the fourth quarter.

Near-Term Fee-Income Headwinds

Management expects roughly $700,000 of one-time items, including CRA-related income, to drop out in the fourth quarter. Gains on loan sales should also be somewhat softer, though overall fee income is expected to remain at a level broadly consistent with the third quarter.

Subordinated Debt Expense and Margin

The fourth quarter will be the first period fully reflecting interest expense on the $100 million subordinated debt issuance. Management noted that this cost will partially offset the typical 1 to 2 basis-point margin lift associated with a 25-basis-point rate hike, tempering near-term NIM upside.

Shared National Credit Portfolio Reduction

Shared national credit exposure declined from about $1 billion to $936 million quarter over quarter. The reduction stemmed from routine renewals and deliberate decisions to avoid certain deals where cross-sell opportunities, expected returns, hold levels, pricing, or risk profiles were not attractive.

Forward-Looking Guidance and Outlook

Looking ahead, management expects mid-single-digit loan growth in the fourth quarter, with full-year net charge-offs of 38 to 40 basis points and a longer-term normalized range of 20 to 25 basis points. Margin should remain stable in Q4 with a modest lift in 2027, expenses are projected to rise 3% to 5% next year, fee income to grow 8% to 10% in 2027, and share repurchases to stay elevated.

In sum, First Merchants delivered a positive earnings story, driven by margin expansion, solid revenue growth, and a well-capitalized balance sheet. While loan growth moderated, mortgage demand softened, and credit activity remained elevated, management’s guidance and commitment to strategic continuity suggest the bank is positioned to sustain attractive returns for investors over the medium term.

Based on current pipelines and unfunded commitments, management expects mid-single-digit annualized loan growth for the next few quarters. Higher five-year rates are also enhancing the asset repricing tailwind, positioning net interest margin and net interest income to continue drifting higher.

Investment in Commercial Online Banking

Nonaccrual loans increased by $16.6 million to just over $32 million, or 0.55% of total loans, versus 0.27% in Q1 and 0.44% at year-end 2025. Higher Criticized Loan Balances

The increase reflected $12.9 million of special-mention loans and a $3 million rise in substandard credits, with notable additions from two construction-related C&I relationships and a multifamily project with slower lease-up.

Increase in Credit-Loss Provision

The bank recorded a $2.3 million provision for credit losses in Q3, tied to strong loan growth and specific reserves for new nonaccrual loans. Roughly $1 million of that provision was directly related to credits that migrated into nonaccrual status during the quarter.

Competitive Pricing Pressure in Lending

Heritage described an increasingly aggressive pricing environment as banks vie for business, particularly in affordable housing. Of the $103 million of projects that left its pipeline, three were shelved and four were lost to competitors offering better terms, underscoring margin pressure on new loans.

Emerging Upward Pressure on Deposit Costs

After an extended period of stable funding costs, management said deposit pricing likely reached an inflection point in Q3. The spot cost of interest-bearing deposits was 1.66% at September-end, and executives cautioned that attracting incremental balances is becoming harder amid intense market competition.

Lower Average Balances on New Accounts

New deposit accounts opened in Q3 carried average balances of about $52 million, down from $62 million in Q2, even as the deposit pipeline grew to $97 million. The trend suggests that while new relationships are being added, the immediate funding benefit from each is moderating.

TCE Ratio Pressure from Unrealized Losses

Heritage’s tangible common equity ratio dipped to 9.3% from 9.7% in the prior quarter, largely because of higher net unrealized losses in its available-for-sale portfolio. Investment balances fell $32 million sequentially as those unrealized losses widened, reflecting rate movements in the bond market.

Expected Increase in Core Expenses

While reported noninterest costs will fall post-merger, management warned that underlying core expenses will move higher over time. Drivers include compensation and benefit inflation, payroll taxes, rising medical premiums, and recurring price increases from third-party service providers, plus technology-related spending.

Reduced Near-Term Share Buyback Activity

Despite having authorization to repurchase up to 5% of outstanding shares, the bank plans to slow buyback activity in Q4. Executives cited the elevated CRE concentration at about 308% and other capital priorities as reasons to be more selective about returning capital to shareholders.

Forward-Looking Guidance and Outlook

Looking ahead, Heritage expects Q4 expenses to land between $55 million and $56 million, even as core costs gradually rise with technology investments, including commercial online banking conversion spending. Management anticipates mid-single-digit annualized loan growth for the next few quarters, continued reinvestment of securities cash flows at higher yields, a further grind higher in net interest margin and net interest income, and a more restrained approach to buybacks in the near term.

Heritage Financial’s call painted a picture of a bank benefiting from rising loan and securities yields, solid loan and deposit growth, and successful merger execution. At the same time, management’s measured tone on credit trends, CRE concentration, competitive pressures, and future expense growth offers investors a balanced view of both the opportunities and the emerging risks ahead.

Waste Connections ((TSE:WCN)) has held its Q3 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call.

Waste Connections struck a notably upbeat tone on its latest earnings call. Management highlighted better-than-expected Q3 results, expanding margins despite fuel headwinds, strong cash generation and balance sheet flexibility. They acknowledged pockets of weakness, including soft volumes, plastics recycling and residential construction, but framed these as manageable within a robust long-term growth and capital-return story.

Q3 Financial Beat Underscores Resilient Core Operations

Third-quarter revenue reached $2.638 billion, up 7.3% year-over-year and above expectations, showing solid top-line momentum despite mixed volumes. Adjusted EBITDA climbed 7.9% to $895.8 million, translating into a 34% margin and reinforcing the company’s ability to defend profitability in a choppy operating environment.

Promotion

55% Off TipRanks

  • Unlock powerful investing tools with TipRanks Premium to make smarter, more confident investment decisions
  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks
Learn more about TipRanks Premium

Margins Expanded Even As Diesel Costs Surged

Underlying adjusted EBITDA margin expanded by 50 basis points, while the reported margin improved 20 basis points to 34% despite a late-quarter spike in diesel. Management said fuel shaved about 30 basis points from margin; excluding that, adjusted EBITDA would have been roughly 34.3%, highlighting strong cost discipline and pricing power.

Pricing And Yield Drive Solid Waste Profitability

Solid waste core pricing stood at a healthy 5.5%, with more modest increases in mostly exclusive Western markets and above 6% in competitive regions. Fuel and material surcharges added about $30 million, or 1.3%, while solid waste yield of 4.3% demonstrated effective rate management even as unit volumes remained negative.

Landfill, Special Waste And C&D Volumes Turn The Corner

Landfill tons rose 3% year-over-year, with rates per ton up around 4%, pointing to improving disposal trends after several sluggish quarters. Special waste climbed 7% and construction and demolition debris increased 5%, marking the first time in recent periods that all three categories showed simultaneous volume gains.

E&P Waste Sees Gradual Recovery, Led By The U.S.

Exploration and production waste revenue increased 6% sequentially and about 5% organically year-over-year, driven by a 9% gain in the U.S. The Permian basin benefited from roughly a 10% rise in rig count since early in the year, although activity still trails prior levels despite higher crude prices.

Recycling And Landfill Gas Deliver Strong Growth

Recycling revenue grew about 12% year-over-year, largely thanks to stronger OCC prices, though plastics remained a notable drag. Landfill gas sales surged 35%, reflecting higher output from new renewable natural gas facilities and roughly 10% higher RIN values, which averaged around $2.50 and boosted the company’s environmental revenue mix.

Raised 2026 Outlook Signals Confidence In Growth Trajectory

Waste Connections lifted its full-year 2026 outlook to about $10.09 billion in revenue and roughly $3.345 billion of adjusted EBITDA, implying a 33.2% margin. The raise reflects Q3 outperformance, incremental acquisition and commodity contributions and an expected easing of current fuel pressures, suggesting management sees continued room for profitable expansion.

Free Cash Flow Track Remains Intact Despite Higher Interest

Year-to-date adjusted free cash flow reached $1.09 billion, in line with internal plans and supporting the forecast of at least $1.4 billion for full-year 2026. Management noted that higher interest expense tied to $1 billion of share repurchases offset some EBITDA upside, limiting flow-through but still leaving substantial cash available for growth and returns.

Acquisition Pipeline And Balance Sheet Support Deal Activity

Acquisitions completed year-to-date represent $130 million of annualized revenue, including two West Coast franchises closed in Q3, and the pipeline remains robust heading into late 2026 and early 2027. Liquidity exceeds $1 billion and leverage sits near 2.75x debt to adjusted EBITDA, giving the company ample capacity to pursue disciplined M&A alongside buybacks.

Dividend Hike And Buybacks Highlight Shareholder Focus

The board approved a 10% increase in the regular quarterly dividend, the 16th straight year of double-digit raises since 2010, underscoring a long track record of capital returns. Year-to-date repurchases of more than $1 billion, or about 2.5% of shares outstanding, further signal confidence in long-term earnings and free cash flow power.

Sustainability And RNG Investments Strengthen Long-Term Moat

The company has spent over $500 million on sustainability-focused projects since 2018 and remains on course to hit its environmental targets, particularly in renewable natural gas and advanced recycling. Management also cited enhanced automation in recycling plants, three straight years of improving employee retention and record safety performance as strategic differentiators.

Constructive 2027 Growth Framework Builds On 2026 Momentum

Management outlined a preliminary 2027 framework calling for mid- to high single-digit revenue growth assuming a steady macro backdrop, including about 1% from acquisitions already completed and RNG projects coming online in 2026. Additional price-led organic growth, surcharges, higher E&P and recycling contributions and further deals underpin this constructive outlook.

Free Cash Flow Per Share Set For Double-Digit Growth

The company expects double-digit growth in adjusted free cash flow per share in 2027 as Chiquita-related spending declines and RNG capital outlays largely wind down. Over time, free cash flow conversion is projected to return to a 48% to 50% range from roughly 42% today, aided by reduced special projects and a pricing strategy that keeps a 150-basis-point edge over costs.

Chiquita Remediation Costs Poised To Step Down

Management reported that Chiquita remediation expenses have already fallen from 2025 to 2026 and should decline again in 2027 as leachate generation and infrastructure needs moderate. Covering and buffering work completed in 2026 will not repeat, and with roughly 300 wells already drilled, the financial drag from the site is expected to fade over the next few years.

Arrowhead And Rail Projects Boost Internalization Efficiency

Arrowhead volumes are now running between 7,000 and 7,500 tons per day, about triple the level less than three years ago, and could reach 8,500 to 9,000 tons within 24 months. Internalization was 58% in the quarter and is expected to stay in the 58% to 60% band, while a Florida rail project continues ramping into 2027, supporting route density and margins.

Disciplined M&A Pace Reflects Market Conditions, Not Constraints

Management emphasized that slower 2026 M&A activity versus 2023–2025 stems from timing and seller behavior, not capital limitations, and that about $200 million of acquired revenue represents a normalized low watermark. They expect acquisition volumes over the next three to five years to resemble the busy 2022–2025 period, maintaining a steady consolidation strategy.

Debt Structure Offers Stability Amid Rate And Fuel Volatility

The company’s debt mix of roughly 80% fixed and 20% floating with an average tenor of about eight years and a 4% cost provides resilience against rate swings. With no near-term maturities, Waste Connections can focus its cash on operations, sustainability projects and capital returns rather than refinancing risk.

AI Initiatives Begin To Support Margins

Early AI-driven operational tools, particularly in pricing, generated benefits in 2025 and 2026 that exceeded management’s expectations. Additional AI programs are under development through 2027, but their incremental margin impact is not yet baked into the 2027 outlook, suggesting potential upside as deployment ramps in 2028 and 2029.

Solid Waste Volumes And Roll-Off Activity Remain Soft

Solid waste unit volumes fell 1.2% year-over-year in Q3, though that marked a 70-basis-point sequential improvement, hinting that the worst may be past. Roll-off pulls declined about 2.5% even as rates per pull rose 5.5%, with volumes down across most regions except the Western U.S., where pulls increased 2.5%.

Fuel Costs And Operating Creep Pressure Margins

Late-quarter diesel spikes caused an estimated 30-basis-point drag on adjusted EBITDA margin, and management warned fuel could remain a headwind in 2027 if prices stay high. They also see fuel-linked cost creep in parts, materials, property expenses and capital repairs, and are weighing diesel hedging for 2027, though current prices complicate lock-in decisions.

Recycling Mix Skewed Toward OCC As Plastics Lag

While higher OCC values underpinned the 12% rise in recycling revenue, the company stressed that plastics remain weak and offset some of that strength. This uneven commodity backdrop means recycling margins depend heavily on fiber markets, adding a layer of volatility to the business despite structural gains from RNG and automation.

Q4 Set To Be Toughest Year-Over-Year Comparison

For Q4, Waste Connections guided to about $2.52 billion of revenue and an adjusted EBITDA margin near 33.3%, implying roughly 20 basis points of underlying margin expansion excluding fuel. Management cautioned that Q4 will be the hardest comparison of the year and said it is too early to assume recent landfill volume improvement will continue without interruption.

C&D And Residential Construction Exposed To Rate Headwinds

In October, special waste stayed positive, but construction and demolition activity did not show the same upturn, reflecting its lumpy and rate-sensitive nature. New housing starts have dropped to about 1.2 million and are expected to move lower given current interest rates, leaving residential construction under pressure from financing, fuel and broader consumer stress.

E&P Activity Trails Crude Prices, Limiting Upside

Despite crude recently touching $100, E&P activity has not fully caught up, with the U.S. rig count up around 10% from earlier in the year but still roughly 50 rigs below prior levels. Producers appear to be treating higher crude prices as non-permanent, keeping drilling and related waste volumes from surging in line with commodity moves.

Interest And Episodic Risk Costs Temper Cash Conversion

Management noted that a roughly $30 million increase in adjusted EBITDA guidance since the year began did not translate into higher free cash flow guidance, largely due to about $40 million of additional interest expense from the accelerated buyback program. The Eastern region also absorbed elevated risk management costs tied to an episodic claim, while other regions saw declines.

Guidance And Long-Term Outlook Emphasize Steady Growth

Looking ahead, Waste Connections sees 2026 revenue around $10.09 billion, adjusted EBITDA of roughly $3.345 billion with a 33.2% margin, and at least $1.4 billion of adjusted free cash flow, with Q4 revenue near $2.52 billion and margins up modestly excluding fuel. For 2027, management expects mid- to high single-digit revenue growth, margin expansion in a normalized range and double-digit free cash flow per share growth, with longer-term conversion returning to 48%–50% as RNG spend rolls off and pricing maintains a 150-basis-point spread over costs.

Waste Connections’ earnings call painted the picture of a company balancing near-term macro and fuel pressures with solid pricing, disciplined costs and growing contributions from sustainability and AI initiatives. For investors, the mix of consistent dividend growth, sizable buybacks, a sturdy balance sheet and a constructive 2027 framework suggests the waste and environmental services specialist remains positioned as a defensive compounder with emerging upside levers.

The bank sees lending potential across regional banking, SBA, private equity, asset-based lending and investor real estate segments. It also added Dan Cuneo to lead Southern New Jersey and Southeastern Pennsylvania, expecting his regional and community banking experience to bolster growth.

Deposit Pricing Pressure

Competition for deposits has intensified following the recent rate increases, with pricing pressure accelerating. Management expects deposit rates to move higher as rivals compete more aggressively, which will in turn push up funding costs.

Decline in Point-to-Point Noninterest-Bearing Deposits

Noninterest-bearing deposits declined by $48.7 million between June 30 and September 30, reflecting both normal fluctuations and rate-driven shifts. Executives warned that rising pricing pressure is likely to lift interest-bearing costs and weigh on noninterest-bearing balances over time.

Margin Headwinds from Accretion and Deposit Competition

Management noted that acquisition-related accretion income will fade, removing a tailwind from the margin. They also expect some of the benefit from asset repricing to be offset as deposit rates rise, making competitive funding costs a key margin headwind.

Higher Net Charge-Offs and Business Express Losses

Net charge-offs ticked up to $1.9 million from $1.6 million in the second quarter, largely due to Business Express exposures. Year-to-date charge-offs of about $8.5 million, 95% from that portfolio, remain above management’s comfort level, and they do not expect credit costs in that book to fall to zero.

Slight Increase in Nonperforming Assets

Nonperforming assets rose modestly to $35.7 million during the quarter, signaling a small uptick in problem credits. Management said NPAs have moved down since quarter end and that some early credit indicators have started to improve.

Noninterest expense of $20.3 million was modestly above the second quarter, mainly due to salaries and benefits. The increase reflected an extra day in the quarter, staffing for the summer intern program and somewhat higher incentive compensation.

Noninterest Income Remains Limited

Noninterest income slipped to $2.0 million from $2.1 million in the prior quarter, reiterating its limited role in the revenue mix. Management does not foresee meaningful short-term changes, leaving net interest income as the primary earnings driver.

Investor Real Estate Loan Decline

Investor real estate loans, a major business line, declined somewhat in the third quarter as the bank prioritized C&I growth. The shift reflects a tactical focus on higher-yielding commercial relationships while keeping real estate exposure in check.

Potential Commercial Real Estate Sensitivity to Higher Rates

Management cautioned that higher interest rates could prompt renegotiations of deals, slow new projects and force borrowers to rework project economics. While no major pullback has emerged recently, another rate increase could pose incremental risk to commercial real estate activity.

Outlook and Forward-Looking Guidance

Looking ahead, First Bank expects Business Express losses to moderate, with segment profitability possible if credit costs normalize to more reasonable annualized levels. The bank anticipates keeping its tax rate at or below 25%, seeing a stable margin with slight upside, better loan yields into the fourth quarter and loan growth of about $300 million in 2027 alongside improved efficiency and profitability.

Third Coast Bancshares Inc ((TCBX)) has held its Q3 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call.

Third Coast Bancshares’ latest earnings call struck a broadly upbeat tone despite softer headline numbers. Executives emphasized strong deposit and loan growth, record tangible book value and stable credit costs. They argued that underlying profitability remains solid once merger-related charges are stripped out, and that strategic moves like securitizations and the Great Plains deal are positioning the bank for longer-term growth.

Underlying Earnings Hold Up Despite Merger Drag

Third Coast reported third-quarter net income of $19 million, down from $22 million in the prior quarter and $18.1 million a year ago. Diluted EPS slipped to $0.93 from $1.08. However, excluding $3.2 million of merger expenses, adjusted net income was about $21.6 million, or $1.06 per share, underscoring solid core performance even as integration costs weigh on reported results.

Noninterest-Bearing Deposits Power Funding Strength

Deposit trends remained a key positive, with noninterest-bearing balances jumping 60.3% over the past year versus 35.5% growth in total deposits. Total deposits ended the quarter at $5.9 billion, up $69 million from June. Noninterest-bearing demand deposits rose about $78 million to $721 million and now represent 12.2% of total deposits, providing a valuable low-cost funding base.

Loan Growth Robust After Securitization Adjustments

Gross loans finished the quarter around $5.5 billion, up $57 million from June despite active loan sales. After excluding about $87 million of loans sold via securitization, underlying loan growth exceeded $144 million. Management added that loans had increased roughly $80 million in the month through the date of the call, reflecting strong origination momentum.

Securitization Becomes a Core Balance Sheet Tool

Management said securitization is now embedded in its broader balance sheet and capital strategy rather than a one-off tactic. Another deal is expected in the fourth quarter, this time backed by commercial loans, which would be a first for the bank. While the latest transaction was modestly negative to quarterly noninterest income net of expenses, executives view it as strategically valuable.

Credit Costs Stay Low With Net Recoveries

Credit performance remained steady, with net recoveries of $27,000 in the quarter, marking a third consecutive period of net recoveries. Year-to-date net recoveries totaled $182,000. The allowance for credit losses increased to $54.4 million, or 0.99% of total loans, signaling management’s continued conservative stance even as actual loss experience remains benign.

Diversified Portfolio and Tight Underwriting Support Resilience

Third Coast highlighted its diversified loan book across industries and geographies, which management believes reduces risk. Commercial and industrial loans account for 43% of total loans, while construction and land represent 16%, owner-occupied CRE 11% and nonowner-occupied CRE 18%. Executives reiterated disciplined underwriting, careful loan structures and proactive monitoring as key safeguards.

Tangible Book Value Hits Record Levels

Shareholder equity metrics improved again, with book value per common share rising to $36.53. Tangible book value per share reached a record $33.31, up from $33.08 at June 30 and $30.91 a year earlier. This steady build in tangible capital offers investors a buffer against economic uncertainty and supports future growth initiatives.

Great Plains Merger to Boost Scale and Reach

The planned merger with Great Plains Bancshares is set to create a roughly $9 billion-asset franchise. The deal expands Third Coast’s footprint in Dallas and opens a new market in Oklahoma. Management expects the combined platform to strengthen commercial banking capabilities, increase capacity to support growth and improve funding through Great Plains’ relationship-driven core deposits.

Integration Benefits From System Compatibility

Early integration work with Great Plains has been encouraging, aided by common technology and treasury platforms. Great Plains operates on FIS, similar to Third Coast, which should simplify conversion compared with the prior Keystone deal. Management described the teams as a natural fit and plans to retain the Great Plains name locally while offering customers a broader product set.

Treasury and Fee Initiatives Start to Gain Traction

Third Coast’s treasury management unit continues to add relationships and open accounts at a brisk pace. Third-quarter fee income was helped by stronger swap fees, loan-related charges and roughly $150,000 of trailing revenue from a previously sold factoring business. Management lifted its quarterly fee-income expectation to around $5 million, noting core fees should climb as the bank grows.

Targeted Hiring Delivers Quick Pipeline Impact

Recently recruited experienced banking teams are already feeding the loan pipeline, with some turning profitable within their first month. The strategy favors fewer, more productive hires over large team additions. Despite growth in talent, salary expense has held around $25 million for three straight quarters, with new costs offset by savings from the Keystone and factoring exits.

Commercial and Industrial Lending Leads Pipeline Strength

Loan pipelines remain strong across business lines but are particularly robust in commercial and industrial lending. New lenders are largely focused on C&I opportunities, positioning this segment for outsized growth. Management added that greater utilization of existing credit lines could also contribute to loan expansion in coming quarters.

Margin Pressured Now, But Recovery Expected

Net interest margin fell to 3.70% from 3.83% last quarter and would have been 3.74% without accelerated accretion. The decline stemmed from lower securitization fees, a low-yield securities book, Keystone premium amortization and payoffs of premium loans. Despite this, management expects margin to rebound in the fourth quarter, citing preliminary September levels of 3.85% and asset sensitivity.

Merger Expenses Set to Ease Near Term

Keystone-related costs are nearly complete, with about $12.5 million of the projected $13 million already spent. Fourth-quarter merger expenses are forecast at roughly $500,000, with an upper bound of $1 million. More material costs for the Great Plains deal are expected to land in the first quarter, but management views the near-term drag as manageable.

Core Deposit and Market-Share Upside From Great Plains

The Great Plains combination is expected to accelerate growth in stable, core deposits, especially in rural markets and North Texas. Great Plains has shown a strong track record of deposit expansion. The enlarged North Texas presence is seen as a key opportunity to gain share in attractive commercial markets while deepening relationship-based funding.

Systems Enable Larger Relationship Accounts

Third Coast now services 25 accounts with balances above $1 million, reflecting the capabilities of its upgraded systems. Management said these higher-grade platforms make it possible to onboard and manage such sizable relationships efficiently. Under legacy systems, the bank likely could not have handled these accounts at the same scale or sophistication.

Headline Earnings and EPS Reflect Merger Costs

Reported earnings showed pressure, with third-quarter net income declining to $19 million from $22 million in the second quarter. Diluted EPS similarly slipped to $0.93 from $1.08. Management emphasized that the quarter included $3.2 million of merger-related charges, underscoring that much of the sequential decline was tied to strategic integration work rather than core operations.

Securitization and Margin Headwinds Weigh on Income

The latest securitization was described as a push at best and slightly negative to noninterest income less expenses, excluding earnings from retained interests. The transaction closed soon after the quarter began, exacerbating the drag. Combined with a lower-yield securities portfolio and loan premium amortization, these factors contributed to the unexpected margin compression.

Efficiency Ratio Rises With One-Off Items

The reported efficiency ratio climbed to 63.1%, with an adjusted level of 58.63%, up from 56.5% in the prior quarter. Management linked the weaker comparison to merger-related and other nonrecurring items, as well as last quarter’s roughly $3.5 million gain from the factoring business sale. Investors were reminded that underlying efficiency remains a focus as integration progresses.

Nonperformers Tick Up but Stay Manageable

Nonperforming loans edged higher to about $29 million from $27.1 million in June. As a share of total loans, NPLs rose slightly to 0.53% from 0.50% and 0.52% a year earlier. The increase was mainly due to three SBA loans totaling around $2.3 million being moved to nonaccrual, a modest change that management does not see as indicative of broader credit deterioration.

Fee Income Still Volatile Despite Upward Trend

Management cautioned that fee income remains lumpy and hard to predict quarter to quarter. Swap fees depend heavily on customer activity, and loan fee income hinges on origination volumes. While executives are optimistic about a higher baseline, they do not expect fee income to reach $6 million every quarter, particularly in the near term.

Great Plains Closing and Cost Saves Not Fully Visible Yet

The closing date for Great Plains is not yet fixed, with management’s best estimate falling between early February and early April. The timing of cost savings will depend on when system conversions occur, and only about half of the expected savings are anticipated to show up in 2027. Investors may need patience before the full economic benefits are evident.

Loan Growth Outlook Tempered by Rate Environment

Management kept its existing loan growth guidance intact, even with strong pipelines across segments. Executives acknowledged that higher interest rates could dampen some loan production. However, they believe the strength of current pipelines and new lender contributions should offset the rate headwind and keep growth near targets.

Forward-Looking Guidance Points to Margin Rebound

Looking ahead, management expects net interest margin to reach around 3.80% in the fourth quarter and expressed hope of outperforming that level. Loans are projected to grow in the $100 million range while executing another securitization, likely in December or early next year. Fee income is guided to about $5 million, merger expenses around $500,000 to $1 million, and salary costs a bit higher, with the Great Plains closing targeted between early February and early April.

Third Coast Bancshares’ earnings call painted a picture of a bank in transition but on solid footing. Core profitability, deposit strength and loan momentum are counterbalancing temporary margin and merger headwinds. For investors, the key takeaway is that management is using strategic deals, securitizations and targeted hiring to build a higher-value franchise, even if reported numbers remain choppy near term.

data.description:
Hexcel Corporation ((HXL)) has held its Q3 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call.

Hexcel Corporation’s latest earnings call struck an optimistic tone, with management emphasizing strong commercial aerospace growth, rising margins, and improving cash generation. While defense and space sales were weaker and near-term inefficiencies weighed on profitability, executives highlighted robust demand signals, expanding capacity, and a clear path to higher long-term margins and revenue.

Strong Third-Quarter Revenue and Earnings Growth

Hexcel reported third-quarter sales of $496 million, up 9% year over year, underscoring solid top-line momentum. Adjusted operating margin improved to 11.0% from 9.8%, while adjusted diluted EPS climbed to $0.50 from $0.37, a 35% increase driven by higher volume, better pricing, and a lower tax rate.

Promotion

  • Unlock powerful investing tools with TipRanks Premium to make smarter, more confident investment decisions
  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks
